grammar.title: Literary inversion and fronting
grammar.explanation_pt:
Além da inversão após expressões negativas (C1), o inglês formal e literário usa outros tipos de **fronting** (deslocar um elemento para o início) com **inversão do sujeito e do verbo**:

**1. Expressões de lugar / movimento + verbo + sujeito** (verbos intransitivos como come, go, stand, lie, sit, walk):
- "**Here comes** the bus." / "**There goes** my chance."
- "**Into the room walked** the president." / "**On the hill stood** an old church."
- "**Beneath the city lie** the remains of a Roman fort."
⚠️ Com pronome, **não** inverta: "Here **it comes**" (não "Here comes it").

**2. Particípio / adjetivo no início + be + sujeito:**
- "**Gone are the days** when..." (Os dias em que... já se foram)
- "**Equally important is** the question of..." / "**Of particular concern is**..."
- "**Attached is** a copy of the contract." / "**Enclosed are**..."
- "**Far more serious was** the damage to his reputation."

**3. Such / So + inversão** (resultado intenso):
- "**Such is** the power of television **that** elections are often won on screen."
- "**So great was** the demand **that** tickets sold out in minutes."
- "**Such was** his influence **that** no one dared to contradict him."

**4. Nowhere / Seldom / Rarely + comparativo:**
- "**Nowhere is** the divide **more** visible **than** in our cities."
- "**Rarely has** a speech had **such** an impact."

**5. So / Neither / Nor + auxiliar + sujeito** (concordância):
- "The president supported the law, **as did** most of the parliament." (as + auxiliar + sujeito — formal)
- "He didn't apologize, **nor did** he resign."

**6. So it was that...** (narrativo, solene): "**So it was that** a small protest became a national movement."

**Efeito:** dramaticidade, ênfase e ritmo. **Use com moderação**: uma ou duas por parágrafo são impactantes; mais que isso soa teatral.

listening.title: Ethos, pathos, logos — and kairos
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de retórica fala sobre os elementos da persuasão.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: You may have heard of Aristotle's three modes of persuasion: ethos, the character and credibility of the speaker; pathos, the emotions of the audience; and logos, the logic of the argument. Less well known, but no less important, is a fourth concept the Greeks discussed: kairos, the opportune moment. Such is the importance of timing that the same words can inspire a nation on one day and fall completely flat on another. Think of a leader addressing the country after a disaster. Rarely is an audience more ready to listen, and rarely does a speaker have more power — or more responsibility. Gone, of course, are the days when a speech reached people only once, in a hall or on the radio. Today, every phrase can be clipped, replayed and reinterpreted in a different context, months or years later. Kairos has become far more complicated. A sentence that was perfectly judged at the time may sound tone-deaf when it resurfaces. Nowhere is this more evident than on social media.

reading.title: The age of the soundbite
reading.text: Gone are the days when political arguments unfolded over hours. In nineteenth-century America, the famous debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas could last three hours, with each candidate speaking for an hour or more while crowds stood and listened. Such was the appetite for political oratory that newspapers printed the speeches in full, and readers studied them line by line. The contrast with today could hardly be sharper. Studies of American television news have documented a dramatic shrinking of the "soundbite" — the length of time a candidate is shown speaking without interruption. According to research frequently cited by media scholars, the average soundbite on the evening news fell from more than forty seconds in the late 1960s to under ten seconds by the end of the 1980s. Social media has accelerated the trend still further. Today, a political career can be made or broken by a phrase short enough to fit on a placard. What has been lost? Critics argue that complexity is the first casualty. Few serious problems — climate change, healthcare, inequality — can be explained in a single sentence, and politicians who attempt to do so are forced to oversimplify. Equally worrying is the effect on public trust. When every statement is designed to be clipped and shared, politicians speak less to persuade than to avoid giving their opponents ammunition. Yet it would be wrong to romanticize the past. Long speeches were by no means guaranteed to be wise, and many nineteenth-century orators were skilled demagogues. Nor is brevity always a vice: some of the most powerful phrases in political history are also among the shortest. Perhaps the real question is not how long political speech should be, but whether audiences still have the patience — and the platforms — to hear arguments that cannot be reduced to a slogan.

questions.q: How long could the Lincoln–Douglas debates last?
questions.answer: Up to three hours.

questions.q: How did the average TV soundbite change, according to research?
questions.answer: From over forty seconds in the late 1960s to under ten seconds by the late 1980s.

questions.q: What two negative effects are mentioned?
questions.answer: Loss of complexity and loss of public trust.

questions.q: Why shouldn't we romanticize the past, according to the writer?
questions.answer: Long speeches weren't always wise; many orators were demagogues; brevity isn't always bad.

writing.model:
The disappearing public square

Gone are the days when a town's most important conversations took place in its square. For centuries, the praça was where Brazilians met, argued, celebrated and protested. Today, those conversations have largely moved online — and our democracy is the poorer for it.

Such is the convenience of social media that it has become, for millions of people, the main source of political information. It is easy to see why. Platforms are free, immediate and available at any hour. Yet they were not designed to foster debate. They were designed to capture attention, and nothing captures attention quite like outrage.

Nowhere is the consequence more visible than in the tone of our political life. Opponents are no longer people with different views but enemies to be defeated. Nuance is punished; certainty is rewarded. A politician who admits doubt is mocked, while one who shouts is shared.

Equally troubling is the fragmentation of reality itself. In the old square, people heard the same speeches, read the same newspapers and, even when they disagreed, argued about the same facts. Online, each of us inhabits a separate world, shaped by algorithms we do not understand. So complete has this separation become that neighbours may now hold entirely different beliefs about events that happened in their own street.

None of this means we should abandon technology, nor should we romanticize a past that excluded many voices. But it does mean we must deliberately rebuild spaces — physical and digital — where citizens can encounter one another as people rather than profiles: public libraries, community meetings, local newspapers, platforms designed for discussion rather than division.

On the walls of many old town halls hangs an image of citizens gathered in a square, listening to one another. It is worth asking whether our grandchildren will understand what it means. Democracy, after all, is not only a system of voting. It is a habit of talking — and habits, once lost, are hard to recover.

grammar.title: The language of spin
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Eufemismos** — palavras suaves para realidades duras:
- **Trabalho:** downsizing, rightsizing, restructuring, letting people go, workforce adjustment, "exploring other opportunities" (= demitido)
- **Economia:** negative growth (= recessão), revenue enhancement (= aumento de impostos), price adjustment (= aumento de preço), correction (= queda)
- **Guerra:** collateral damage, neutralize, friendly fire, enhanced interrogation
- **Vida pessoal:** passed away, between jobs, economically disadvantaged
⚠️ Nem todo eufemismo é manipulação: "passed away" é **delicadeza**; "collateral damage" pode **desumanizar**.

**2. Weasel words** — criam a **impressão** de uma afirmação sem afirmar nada verificável:
- **Fontes vagas:** "Some experts say...", "Studies show...", "It is widely believed...", "Many people are saying..."
- **Qualificadores:** "**up to** 70% off" (pode ser 5%), "**helps** reduce" (não diz quanto), "**virtually** invisible", "**can** improve", "**as much as**"
- **Comparações incompletas:** "**40% more** effective" (do que o quê?)

**3. Gramática para ocultar o agente:**
- **Passiva sem agente:** "Mistakes **were made**." / "The data **was lost**." / "Shots **were fired**."
- **Nominalização:** "There has been **a reduction in staff**" (em vez de "We fired 300 people")
- **Verbos ergativos** (sem agente): "The project **failed**." / "Prices **rose**." / "The ship **sank**."
- **Sujeitos abstratos:** "**The situation** has led to job losses."

**4. O falso pedido de desculpas (non-apology):**
- "I'm sorry **if** anyone was offended." (coloca a culpa em quem se ofendeu)
- "I regret that **you feel** that way."
- "Mistakes were made, **but** ..."
- Um pedido real: "**I** was wrong. **I** apologize for **what I said**. **It** won't happen again."

**Antídoto C2:** pergunte sempre **quem fez o quê, a quem, quanto e segundo quem?**

listening.title: Politics and the English language
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de literatura fala sobre o ensaio de George Orwell sobre linguagem política.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: In 1946, George Orwell published an essay called "Politics and the English Language". His argument was that political language is often designed to make the indefensible sound reasonable. He gave examples from his own time: villages bombed and inhabitants driven out were described as "pacification". Rather than describe brutal events directly, officials reached for abstract, Latinate words that created a kind of fog. Orwell also attacked lazy writing more generally — dying metaphors, pretentious vocabulary, unnecessary passives — because he believed that sloppy language makes sloppy thinking easier. He ended with six rules, the most famous of which is probably: "Never use a long word where a short one will do." He was also honest enough to add a final rule allowing writers to break any of the others rather than say anything outright barbarous. Almost eighty years later, the essay is still widely read, and its central warning still applies. When language stops describing reality and starts concealing it, democracy has a problem.

reading.title: The anatomy of a non-apology
reading.text: Few genres of public communication have been studied as closely, or mocked as mercilessly, as the corporate apology. When a company is caught polluting a river, mistreating customers or leaking personal data, its statement tends to follow a predictable pattern — one that linguists and public relations experts have learned to dissect. It typically begins with an expression of regret, rather than an apology: "We regret any inconvenience this may have caused." The verb "regret" is significant. One can regret a storm; regret does not imply responsibility. The phrase "any inconvenience" minimizes the harm, while "may have caused" leaves open the possibility that nothing was caused at all. Next comes the passive voice. "Mistakes were made" and "data was accessed" describe events without naming anyone who performed them. The agent — the company, its executives, a specific decision — quietly vanishes from the sentence. Then there is the conditional apology: "We apologize to anyone who was affected" or "We're sorry if customers felt let down." By placing the problem in the reactions of others, the statement implies that the fault lies, at least partly, in their sensitivity. Finally, the statement moves swiftly to the future: "We are committed to the highest standards and are reviewing our processes." The past, with all its awkward details, is left behind. Research on apologies suggests that the most effective ones do almost exactly the opposite. They acknowledge responsibility clearly, name the specific harm, express genuine remorse, explain what went wrong and offer concrete repair. They are short, specific and active. "We broke your trust. Here is what we did, here is why it happened, and here is what we will do to put it right." Such apologies are rare, not because they are hard to write, but because they are hard to say. They require something the language of spin is designed to avoid: accepting the blame.

grammar.title: Formal connectives
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Concessão formal:**
- **notwithstanding** (= despite / however) — antes ou depois do substantivo: "**Notwithstanding** the delay, the project was completed." / "The delay **notwithstanding**, ..."; também advérbio: "It was expensive; it was, **notwithstanding**, a success."
- **albeit** (= although) + adjetivo/advérbio/frase sem verbo: "a significant, **albeit** temporary, improvement" / "He agreed, **albeit** reluctantly."
- **be that as it may** (C1) / **that said** / **nonetheless**

**2. Extensão / grau:**
- **insofar as / in so far as** (= to the extent that): "The plan is fair **insofar as** everyone pays the same."
- **inasmuch as** (= since / to the extent that, formal): "He is responsible **inasmuch as** he signed the document."

**3. Meio / relação:**
- **whereby** (= by which, através do qual): "a system **whereby** employees can buy shares"
- **wherein / whereupon**: "the document **wherein** the terms are stated" / "He signed, **whereupon** the meeting ended." (= depois do que)

**4. Resultado / consequência:**
- **hence** (= portanto / daí) — muitas vezes sem verbo: "The data were incomplete, **hence** the delay."
- **thus** (= assim, portanto): "Costs fell; **thus**, prices could be reduced."
- **thereby** + -ing (= com isso, desse modo): "The bank raised rates, **thereby** reducing inflation."

**5. Finalidade negativa:**
- **lest** + (should) + verbo base (= para que não, formal/literário): "Keep a copy **lest** the original **be** lost."
- **for fear that / for fear of** + -ing: "He kept quiet **for fear of** losing his job."

**6. Linguagem jurídica (here- / there-):**
- **hereby** (por meio deste), **herein** (neste documento), **hereinafter** (doravante denominado), **thereof** (dele/disso), **therein** (nele)
- "The Company (**hereinafter** "the Provider") **hereby** agrees..."

⚠️ **Use com critério:** em e-mails comuns, "hereby" e "lest" soam arcaicos. São adequados em **textos jurídicos, acadêmicos e muito formais**.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: Almost everyone clicks "I agree" without reading. In one well-known experiment, published in 2016, researchers Jonathan Obar and Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch created a fictitious social network and asked students to sign up. Buried in the terms of service was a clause whereby users agreed to give up their first-born child as payment. The overwhelming majority of participants agreed — most of them, apparently, without noticing. The study was, admittedly, an exaggeration, albeit a revealing one. Real terms of service rarely demand children, but they frequently contain provisions whereby users waive important rights: allowing companies to share data with third parties, to change the terms at any time, or to resolve disputes through private arbitration rather than in court. Several jurisdictions, including the European Union, have introduced rules requiring that key information be presented clearly, thereby giving consumers a better chance of understanding what they're signing. Notwithstanding these efforts, the basic problem remains: terms are long, readers are busy, and the default is to trust.

reading.title: In defence of legalese?
reading.text: Few styles of writing are as widely disliked as "legalese": the dense, archaic and seemingly impenetrable language of contracts, statutes and terms of service. Critics have long argued that it serves mainly to exclude ordinary readers, thereby protecting the interests of lawyers and the powerful. Movements for "plain language" in law have won significant victories, and in many countries, government documents and consumer contracts must now be written in a way that the average reader can understand. Yet legal language is not merely the product of tradition or self-interest. Many of its peculiarities exist for a reason. Words such as "notwithstanding", "hereinafter" and "whereby" allow drafters to establish precise relationships between different parts of a document — which clause overrides which, how a term is defined, by what mechanism an obligation arises. Ordinary words, by contrast, tend to be vague, and vagueness in a contract can lead to years of costly litigation. Repetition, too, has a purpose: a lawyer who writes "the Buyer" fifty times rather than switching to "they" or "the customer" ensures that no court can later argue that the parties meant different people. Some features, admittedly, are harder to defend. Doublets and triplets such as "null and void", "cease and desist" and "give, devise and bequeath" are largely historical relics, dating from a time when English law drew on English, French and Latin and drafters used all three to be safe. Long sentences with multiple embedded clauses serve the convenience of the writer far more than the comprehension of the reader. The challenge, then, is not to abolish legal language but to distinguish precision from obscurity. A good contract should be as exact as necessary — albeit no more complicated than it needs to be. Insofar as plain language can achieve that, it is not the enemy of the law but its ally.

warmup.text_pt: "**Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.**" (John F. Kennedy, 1961). Por que essa frase sobreviveu mais de 60 anos? grammar.title: Rhetorical figures
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Paralelismo** — estruturas gramaticais **iguais** em sequência (a base de quase todas as figuras):
- ❌ "She likes swimming, to run and cycles." ✅ "She likes **swimming, running and cycling**."
- "We will **build** schools, **train** teachers and **support** families."

**2. Tricolon** (C1, revisão): três elementos paralelos, geralmente com o último mais longo ou forte.
- "government **of** the people, **by** the people, **for** the people" (Lincoln, 1863)

**3. Anáfora** — repetição no **início** de frases/orações:
- "**We shall fight** on the beaches, **we shall fight** on the landing grounds, **we shall fight** in the fields..." (Churchill, 1940)

**4. Epístrofe** — repetição no **final**:
- "...government of the people, by the **people**, for the **people**."
- "When I was a child, I spoke as a **child**, I understood as a **child**, I thought as a **child**." (Bíblia, King James)

**5. Antítese** — ideias opostas em estrutura paralela:
- "...**not because** they are **easy**, **but because** they are **hard**." (Kennedy, 1962)
- "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind." (Armstrong, 1969)

**6. Quiasmo** — repetição **invertida** (A-B / B-A):
- "Ask not what **your country** can do for **you** — ask what **you** can do for **your country**." (Kennedy, 1961)
- "**Eat** to **live**, not **live** to **eat**."
- "It's not the **years** in your **life**, it's the **life** in your **years**."

**7. Aliteração e assonância** — repetição de sons: "**b**igger, **b**etter, **b**older"; "**p**eace, **p**rosperity and **p**rogress"

**8. Perguntas retóricas e pausas** (C1, revisão).

**Gramática do paralelismo:** ao listar ações, mantenha a **mesma forma** (todos verbos base, todos -ing, todos substantivos); ao contrastar, use **estruturas idênticas**: "not X but Y", "less X, more Y", "the more X, the more Y".

grammar.tip_pt: Discursos brasileiros também usam essas figuras — de Rui Barbosa aos sambas-enredo. Ao escrever em inglês, comece pelo **paralelismo**: ele torna frases mais claras **e** mais memoráveis. As figuras mais sofisticadas (quiasmo, epístrofe) funcionam melhor **uma vez**, no momento de maior impacto.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em discursos, as figuras retóricas dependem de **ritmo**: pausas iguais entre elementos paralelos, ênfase nas palavras repetidas ou contrastadas, e **desaceleração** na frase final. dialogue.title: Rehearsing the graduation speech
dialogue.context_pt: Uma estudante ensaia o discurso de formatura com um professor de oratória.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Let's hear your closing paragraph, Luana.
lines.pt: Vamos ouvir seu parágrafo final, Luana.

lines.speaker: Luana
lines.en: "We learned a lot here. We made friends and we had good teachers. Now we have to go out and change things."
lines.pt: "Aprendemos muito aqui. Fizemos amigos e tivemos bons professores. Agora temos que sair e mudar as coisas."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: It's sincere, but it won't stay with anyone. Try parallelism. What did this place give you?
lines.pt: É sincero, mas ninguém vai lembrar. Tente paralelismo. O que este lugar te deu?

lines.speaker: Luana
lines.en: "Here, we learned to question. Here, we learned to listen. Here, we learned to fail — and to try again."
lines.pt: "Aqui, aprendemos a questionar. Aqui, aprendemos a ouvir. Aqui, aprendemos a falhar — e a tentar de novo."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Anaphora and a tricolon, with the longest item last. Beautiful. Now the ending — can you use a contrast?
lines.pt: Anáfora e um tricolon, com o item mais longo por último. Lindo. Agora o final — consegue usar um contraste?

lines.speaker: Luana
lines.en: "We did not come here to find answers; we came here to find better questions."
lines.pt: "Não viemos aqui para encontrar respostas; viemos aqui para encontrar perguntas melhores."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Antithesis. And the very last line?
lines.pt: Antítese. E a última linha?

lines.speaker: Luana
lines.en: "For years, this school has been changing us. From today, let us go out and change the world — not for ourselves, but for each other."
lines.pt: "Por anos, esta escola nos transformou. A partir de hoje, vamos sair e transformar o mundo — não por nós mesmos, mas uns pelos outros."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Now slow down on that final sentence, pause before "but", and look up. That's the line they'll remember.
lines.pt: Agora desacelere nessa última frase, faça uma pausa antes do "but" e olhe para o público. É essa a frase que vão lembrar.

listening.title: Anatomy of a famous speech
listening.context_pt: Um historiador analisa o Discurso de Gettysburg, de Abraham Lincoln (1863).

lines.speaker: Historian
lines.en: On 19 November 1863, at the dedication of a military cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, Abraham Lincoln spoke for around two minutes. The main speaker that day, the celebrated orator Edward Everett, had spoken for about two hours. It is Lincoln's speech that is remembered. Why? Partly because of its brevity — fewer than three hundred words — and partly because of its extraordinary craftsmanship. Lincoln uses antithesis repeatedly: the world "will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here." He uses a tricolon of verbs: "we can not dedicate — we can not consecrate — we can not hallow — this ground." And he ends with perhaps the most famous example of epistrophe in American history, describing a government "of the people, by the people, for the people". Notice, too, the irony of that first antithesis: Lincoln claimed the world would not remember his words. Rarely has a prediction been so completely wrong.

questions.q: How long did Lincoln speak, compared with Edward Everett?
questions.answer: About two minutes, compared with about two hours.

questions.q: Give an example of antithesis from the speech.
questions.answer: "The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here."

questions.q: What tricolon of verbs does Lincoln use?
questions.answer: Dedicate, consecrate, hallow.

questions.q: What is ironic about the first antithesis?
questions.answer: Lincoln said the world wouldn't remember his words, but it did.

reading.title: Why rhetoric still matters
reading.text: For much of Western history, rhetoric — the art of persuasive speech — stood at the centre of education. Roman schoolboys practised declamation; medieval universities taught it as one of the three foundational arts, alongside grammar and logic; and well into the nineteenth century, educated people were expected to recognize, and to use, figures such as anaphora and chiasmus. In the twentieth century, however, rhetoric acquired a bad name. After decades of wartime propaganda and, later, the polished manipulations of advertising, the word came to suggest empty or deceptive speech: "mere rhetoric". Many schools quietly dropped it from the curriculum. This is unfortunate, for two reasons. First, the techniques of rhetoric have not disappeared; they have simply become less visible. Every political speech, advertising campaign and viral post draws on the same toolkit that Cicero and Quintilian described two thousand years ago. Citizens who cannot recognize these techniques are, in a sense, defenceless against them. To identify a false antithesis — "either you are with us or you are against us" — is already to begin to resist it. Second, rhetoric is not only a weapon of the powerful. It has also been the instrument of those seeking to challenge power. Abolitionists, suffragists and civil rights leaders were, almost without exception, masters of persuasive language; their speeches combined moral clarity with carefully crafted rhythm, repetition and contrast. To dismiss rhetoric as manipulation is, in effect, to give up one of the most effective tools of democratic change. Perhaps the solution is to return rhetoric to its original place: not as a set of tricks but as a discipline of both speaking and listening. A society that teaches its citizens to recognize persuasion, to analyse it and to use it responsibly is far better equipped to govern itself than one that merely hopes its leaders will speak honestly.

questions.q: What were the three foundational arts in medieval universities?
questions.answer: Grammar, logic and rhetoric.

questions.q: Why did rhetoric acquire a bad name in the twentieth century?
questions.answer: Because of wartime propaganda and advertising manipulation.

questions.q: What is the first reason it's unfortunate to drop rhetoric from education?
questions.answer: The techniques are still used; citizens who can't recognize them are defenceless.

questions.q: What is the second reason?
questions.answer: Rhetoric has also been a tool for challenging power and democratic change.

writing.model:
Opening of the Vila Esperança Community Library

Friends, neighbours, children of Vila Esperança,

Three years ago, on this very spot, there was nothing but a broken wall and a pile of rubbish. Today, there are four thousand books.

They told us it was impossible. They told us there was no money. They told us that nobody here would read. Look around you. Every shelf in this room is an answer to them.

This library was not built by the government, nor by a company, nor by a single generous donor. It was built by you: by the bricklayer who gave his weekends, by the grandmother who organized the book drive, by the teenagers who painted these walls. It was built not with money, but with time; not with promises, but with hands.

Some people say that books belong to the past — that our children need screens, not stories. I say they need both. But a screen can show you the world; a book can show you yourself.

Here, a child who has never left this neighbourhood can travel to the Amazon, to Lisbon, to the moon. Here, an adult who never finished school can finally finish a book. Here, every one of us can find a quiet place in a noisy world.

We did not build this library because it was easy. We built it because it was necessary.

So, to the children of Vila Esperança, I have just one request. Don't just read the books in this room — one day, write the books that will fill it. Because a community that reads can change its story; a community that writes its story can change the world.

Welcome to your library.

— Figures used: anaphora ("They told us...", "Here..."), tricolon (bricklayer, grandmother, teenagers), antithesis (not with money, but with time), chiasmus ("a community that reads can change its story; a community that writes its story..."), parallel antithesis ("not because it was easy... because it was necessary").
